notes: The manual leaves button placement and GPIO choice to the learner. I used the pins from its full code listing: GPIO4 (drum), GPIO17 (cymbal), GPIO27 (snare), GPIO10 (bell).

Each pushbutton straddles the breadboard centre gap. Side 1 (1.l/1.r) is in the top half and side 2 (2.l/2.r) is in the bottom half. The GPIO wire goes to side 1 and the ground jumper goes to side 2. Pressing the button joins the GPIO pin to ground, matching gpiozero Button with its internal pull-up.
The five pin-to-socket leads are modelled as jumper-wire-mf. I assumed port 'a' is the pin end (breadboard) and port 'b' is the socket end (Pi header). Four carry GPIO signals and one carries GND.
The four pin-to-pin jumpers link each button's bottom-half column to the shared bottom negative rail (bn). The GND pin-to-socket lead feeds that rail at bn.1.

The speakers or headphones plug into the Pi's 3.5 mm audio jack (the manual says only 'speakers or headphones'). The raspberry-pi catalogue entry has no audio-jack port, so the speaker is attached with a single joined edge to pi1 with no named ports. The sound is played by the software, so no electrical edge to the GPIO circuit is drawn.
The pygame and gpiozero code steps produce no physical parts.
